     3	ro-crate-py is a Python library to create and consume [Research Object Crates](https://w3id.org/ro/crate). It currently supports the [RO-Crate 1.1](https://w3id.org/ro/crate/1.1) specification.

     6	## Installation
     7	
     8	ro-crate-py requires Python 3.7 or later. The easiest way to install is via [pip](https://docs.python.org/3/installing/):

    17	git clone https://github.com/ResearchObject/ro-crate-py
    18	cd ro-crate-py
    19	pip install .
    20	```
    21	
    22	
    23	## Usage
    24	
    25	### Creating an RO-Crate
    26	
    27	In its simplest form, an RO-Crate is a directory tree with an `ro-crate-metadata.json` file at the top level that contains metadata about the other files and directories, represented by [data entities](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/1.1/data-entities.html). These metadata consist both of properties of the data entities themselves and of other, non-digital entities called [contextual entities](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/1.1/contextual-entities.html) (representing, e.g., a person or an organization).
    28	
    29	Suppose Alice and Bob worked on a research task together, which resulted in a manuscript written by both; additionally, Alice prepared a spreadsheet containing the experimental data, which Bob used to generate a diagram. Let's make an RO-Crate to package all this:
    30	
    31	```python
    32	from rocrate.rocrate import ROCrate
    33	
    34	crate = ROCrate()
    35	paper = crate.add_file("exp/paper.pdf", properties={
    36	    "name": "manuscript",
    37	    "encodingFormat": "application/pdf"
    38	})
    39	table = crate.add_file("exp/results.csv", properties={
    40	    "name": "experimental data",
    41	    "encodingFormat": "text/csv"
    42	})
    43	diagram = crate.add_file("exp/diagram.svg", dest_path="images/figure.svg", properties={
    44	    "name": "bar chart",
    45	    "encodingFormat": "image/svg+xml"
    46	})
    47	```
    48	
    49	We've started by adding the data entities. Now we need contextual entities to represent Alice and Bob:
    50	
    51	```python
    52	from rocrate.model.person import Person
    53	
    54	alice_id = "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
    55	bob_id = "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0001"
    56	alice = crate.add(Person(crate, alice_id, properties={
    57	    "name": "Alice Doe",
    58	    "affiliation": "University of Flatland"
    59	}))
    60	bob = crate.add(Person(crate, bob_id, properties={
    61	    "name": "Bob Doe",
    62	    "affiliation": "University of Flatland"
    63	}))
    64	```
    65	
    66	Next, we express authorship of the various files:

    69	paper["author"] = [alice, bob]
    70	table["author"] = alice
    71	diagram["author"] = bob
    72	```

    77	crate.write("exp_crate")
    78	```
    79	
    80	Now the `exp_crate` directory should contain copies of the three files and an `ro-crate-metadata.json` file with a JSON-LD serialization of the entities and relationships we created, according to the RO-Crate profile. Note that we have chosen a different destination path for the diagram, while the other two files have been placed at the top level with their names unchanged (the default).
    81	
    82	Some applications and services support RO-Crates stored as archives. To save the crate in zip format, use `write_zip`:

    86	```

    88	You can also add whole directories. A directory in RO-Crate is represented by the `Dataset` entity:

    91	logs = crate.add_dataset("exp/logs")
    92	```
    93	
    94	Note that the above adds all files and directories contained in `"exp/logs"` recursively to the crate, but only the top-level `"exp/logs"` dataset itself is listed in the metadata file (there is no requirement to represent every file and folder in the JSON-LD). To also add files and directory recursively to the metadata, use `add_tree` (but note that it only works on local directory trees).
    95	
    96	
    97	#### Appending elements to property values
    98	
    99	What ro-crate-py entities actually store is their JSON representation:
   100	
   101	```python
   102	paper.properties()
   103	```
   104	
   105	```json
   106	{
   107	  "@id": "paper.pdf",
   108	  "@type": "File",
   109	  "name": "manuscript",
   110	  "encodingFormat": "application/pdf",
   111	  "author": [
   112	    {"@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"},
   113	    {"@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0001"},
   114	  ]
   115	}
   116	```

   121	donald = crate.add(Person(crate, "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Duck"))
   122	paper.append_to("author", donald)
   123	```
   124	
   125	Note that `append_to` also works if the property to be updated is missing or has only one value:
   126	
   127	```python
   128	for n in "Mickey_Mouse", "Scrooge_McDuck":
   129	    p = crate.add(Person(crate, f"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/{n}"))
   130	    donald.append_to("follows", p)
   131	```
   132	
   133	#### Adding remote entities
   134	
   135	Data entities can also be remote:
   136	
   137	```python
   138	input_data = crate.add_file("http://example.org/exp_data.zip")
   139	```
   140	
   141	By default the file won't be downloaded, and will be referenced by its URI in the serialized crate:
   142	
   143	```json
   144	{
   145	  "@id": "http://example.org/exp_data.zip",
   146	  "@type": "File"
   147	},
   148	```
   149	
   150	If you add `fetch_remote=True` to the `add_file` call, however, the library (when `crate.write` is called) will try to download the file and include it in the output crate.
   151	
   152	Another option that influences the behavior when dealing with remote entities is `validate_url`, also `False` by default: if it's set to `True`, when the crate is serialized, the library will try to open the URL to add / update metadata bits such as the content's length and format (but it won't try to download the file unless `fetch_remote` is also set).
   153	
   154	
   155	#### Adding entities with an arbitrary type
   156	
   157	An entity can be of any type listed in the [RO-Crate context](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/1.1/context.jsonld). However, only a few of them have a counterpart (e.g., `File`) in the library's class hierarchy (either because they are very common or because they are associated with specific functionality that can be conveniently embedded in the class implementation). In other cases, you can explicitly pass the type via the `properties` argument:
   158	
   159	```python
   160	from rocrate.model.contextentity import ContextEntity
   161	
   162	hackathon = crate.add(ContextEntity(crate, "#bh2021", properties={
   163	    "@type": "Hackathon",
   164	    "name": "Biohackathon 2021",
   165	    "location": "Barcelona, Spain",
   166	    "startDate": "2021-11-08",
   167	    "endDate": "2021-11-12"
   168	}))
   169	```
   170	
   171	Note that entities can have multiple types, e.g.:
   172	
   173	```python
   174	    "@type" = ["File", "SoftwareSourceCode"]
   175	```
   176	
   177	#### Modifying the crate from JSON-LD dictionaries
   178	
   179	The `add_jsonld` method allows to add a contextual entity directly from a
   180	JSON-LD dictionary containing at least the `@id` and `@type` keys:
   181	
   182	```python
   183	crate.add_jsonld({
   184	    "@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000",
   185	    "@type": "Person",
   186	    "name": "Alice Doe"
   187	})
   188	```
   189	
   190	Existing entities can be updated from JSON-LD dictionaries via `update_jsonld`:
   191	
   192	```python
   193	crate.update_jsonld({
   194	    "@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000",
   195	    "name": "Alice K. Doe"
   196	})
   197	```
   198	
   199	There is also an `add_or_update_jsonld` method that adds the entity if it's
   200	not already in the crate and updates it if it already exists (note that, when
   201	updating, the `@type` key is ignored). This allows to "patch" an RO-Crate from
   202	a JSON-LD file. For instance, suppose you have the following `patch.json` file:
   203	
   204	```json
   205	{
   206	    "@graph": [
   207	        {
   208	            "@id": "./",
   209	            "author": {"@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0001"}
   210	        },
   211	        {
   212	            "@id": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0001",
   213	            "@type": "Person",
   214	            "name": "Bob Doe"
   215	        }
   216	    ]
   217	}
   218	```
   219	
   220	Then the following sets Bob as the author of the crate according to the above
   221	file:
   222	
   223	```python
   224	crate = ROCrate("temp-crate")
   225	with open("patch.json") as f:
   226	    json_data = json.load(f)
   227	for d in json_data.get("@graph", []):
   228	    crate.add_or_update_jsonld(d)
   229	```
   230	
   231	### Consuming an RO-Crate
   232	
   233	An existing RO-Crate package can be loaded from a directory or zip file:
   234	
   235	```python
   236	crate = ROCrate('exp_crate')  # or ROCrate('exp_crate.zip')
   237	for e in crate.get_entities():
   238	    print(e.id, e.type)
   239	```
   240	
   241	```
   242	ro-crate-metadata.json CreativeWork
   243	./ Dataset
   244	paper.pdf File
   245	results.csv File
   246	images/figure.svg File
   247	https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000 Person
   248	https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0001 Person
   249	```
   250	
   251	The first two entities shown in the output are the [metadata file descriptor](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/1.1/metadata.html) and the [root data entity](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/1.1/root-data-entity.html), respectively. These are special entities managed by the `ROCrate` object, and are always present. The other entities are the ones we added in the [section on RO-Crate creation](#creating-an-ro-crate). You can access data entities with `crate.data_entities` and contextual entities with `crate.contextual_entities`. For instance:
   252	
   253	```python
   254	for e in crate.data_entities:
   255	    author = e.get("author")
   256	    if not author:
   257	        continue
   258	    elif isinstance(author, list):
   259	        print(e.id, [p["name"] for p in author])
   260	    else:
   261	        print(e.id, repr(author["name"]))
   262	```
   263	
   264	```
   265	paper.pdf ['Alice Doe', 'Bob Doe']
   266	results.csv 'Alice Doe'
   267	images/figure.svg 'Bob Doe'
   268	```
   269	
   270	You can fetch an entity by its `@id` as follows:
   271	
   272	```python
   273	article = crate.dereference("paper.pdf")
   274	```
   275	
   276	
   277	## Command Line Interface
   278	
   279	`ro-crate-py` includes a hierarchical command line interface: the `rocrate` tool. `rocrate` is the top-level command, while specific functionalities are provided via sub-commands. Currently, the tool allows to initialize a directory tree as an RO-Crate (`rocrate init`) and to modify the metadata of an existing RO-Crate (`rocrate add`).
   280	
   281	```console
   282	$ rocrate --help
   283	Usage: rocrate [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
   284	
   285	Options:
   286	  --help  Show this message and exit.
   287	
   288	Commands:
   289	  add
   290	  init
   291	  write-zip
   292	```
   293	
   294	### Crate initialization
   295	
   296	The `rocrate init` command explores a directory tree and generates an RO-Crate metadata file (`ro-crate-metadata.json`) listing all files and directories as `File` and `Dataset` entities, respectively.
   297	
   298	```console
   299	$ rocrate init --help
   300	Usage: rocrate init [OPTIONS]
   301	
   302	Options:
   303	  --gen-preview
   304	  -e, --exclude CSV
   305	  -c, --crate-dir PATH
   306	  --help                Show this message and exit.
   307	```
   308	
   309	The command acts on the current directory, unless the `-c` option is specified. The metadata file is added (overwritten if present) to the directory at the top level, turning it into an RO-Crate.
   310	
   311	### Adding items to the crate
   312	
   313	The `rocrate add` command allows to add workflows and other entity types (currently [testing-related metadata](https://crs4.github.io/life_monitor/workflow_testing_ro_crate)) to an RO-Crate:
   314	
   315	```console
   316	$ rocrate add --help
   317	Usage: rocrate add [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
   318	
   319	Options:
   320	  --help  Show this message and exit.
   321	
   322	Commands:
   323	  test-definition
   324	  test-instance
   325	  test-suite
   326	  workflow
   327	```
   328	
   329	Note that data entities (e.g., workflows) must already be present in the directory tree: the effect of the command is to register them in the metadata file.
   330	
   331	### Example
   332	
   333	```bash
   334	# From the ro-crate-py repository root
   335	cd test/test-data/ro-crate-galaxy-sortchangecase
   336	```
   337	
   338	This directory is already an RO-Crate. Delete the metadata file to get a plain directory tree:
   339	
   340	```bash
   341	rm ro-crate-metadata.json
   342	```
   343	
   344	Now the directory tree contains several files and directories, including a Galaxy workflow and a Planemo test file, but it's not an RO-Crate since there is no metadata file. Initialize the crate:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	rocrate init
   348	```
   349	
   350	This creates an `ro-crate-metadata.json` file that lists files and directories rooted at the current directory. Note that the Galaxy workflow is listed as a plain `File`:

   352	```json

   354	  "@id": "sort-and-change-case.ga",
   355	  "@type": "File"
   356	}
   357	```
   358	
   359	To register the workflow as a `ComputationalWorkflow`:
   360	
   361	```bash
   362	rocrate add workflow -l galaxy sort-and-change-case.ga
   363	```
   364	
   365	Now the workflow has a type of `["File", "SoftwareSourceCode", "ComputationalWorkflow"]` and points to a `ComputerLanguage` entity that represents the Galaxy workflow language. Also, the workflow is listed as the crate's `mainEntity` (see the [Workflow RO-Crate profile](https://w3id.org/workflowhub/workflow-ro-crate/1.0)).

* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.
